title: Indexing deep dive — covering, filtered, fragmentation, missing index DMVs
exp: Index questions at 4 YOE go beyond 'clustered vs non-clustered.' Interviewers expect you to know covering indexes, filtered indexes, when indexes hurt, and how to find missing indexes using DMVs. These come up whenever the interviewer asks 'how would you optimize this query?'
pts: Clustered index: defines the physical sort order of the table (the table IS the B-tree); one per table; lookup is a direct B-tree traversal
Non-clustered index: separate B-tree with key columns + pointer (row locator) to the clustered index or heap; many per table
**Covering index:** an index that includes ALL columns needed by a query (SELECT + WHERE + ORDER BY) — no Key Lookup needed, fastest for read-only queries
**Filtered index:** a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (e.g., `WHERE status = 'active'`) — smaller, faster, more selective for a subset of data
**Key Lookup:** expensive operation in the execution plan when a non-clustered index is used but the query needs columns not in the index — fix by adding an INCLUDE clause
**INCLUDE clause:** adds non-key columns to the leaf level of a non-clustered index for covering without affecting key order: `CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (status) INCLUDE (amount, date)`
**Index fragmentation:** caused by page splits during inserts/updates. Internal fragmentation (pages not full) → REORGANIZE. External fragmentation (page order out of sequence) → REBUILD.
`sys.dm_db_missing_index_details` / `sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups` — DMVs that track queries the optimizer wanted an index for but none existed
**Index maintenance:** REBUILD (offline, full rewrite) vs REORGANIZE (online, incremental defrag). Rebuild when fragmentation > 30%, Reorganize when 10–30%.
Too many indexes hurt write performance — each INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update every index on that table
code:
-- Covering index: include all columns the query needs
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_status_covering
ON orders (status)
INCLUDE (customer_id, amount, order_date);
-- Now: SELECT customer_id, amount, order_date FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'
-- uses index-only scan — no Key Lookup

-- Filtered index: only active orders
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_active
ON orders (customer_id, order_date)
WHERE status = 'active';  -- smaller index, faster for active-only queries

-- Check fragmentation
SELECT
  OBJECT_NAME(ips.object_id) AS table_name,
  i.name AS index_name,
  ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent,
  ips.page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'SAMPLED') ips
JOIN sys.indexes i ON ips.object_id = i.object_id AND ips.index_id = i.index_id
WHERE ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 10
ORDER BY ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent DESC;

-- Rebuild (offline) when fragmentation > 30%
ALTER INDEX ix_orders_status ON orders REBUILD;

-- Reorganize (online) when fragmentation 10-30%
ALTER INDEX ix_orders_status ON orders REORGANIZE;

-- Missing index recommendations
SELECT
  mid.statement AS table_name,
  mid.equality_columns, mid.inequality_columns, mid.included_columns,
  migs.avg_user_impact,  -- % query improvement estimated
  migs.user_seeks + migs.user_scans AS usage_count
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details mid
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups mig ON mid.index_handle = mig.index_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats migs ON mig.index_group_handle = migs.group_handle
ORDER BY migs.avg_user_impact DESC;

qa.q: What is a covering index and how does it eliminate Key Lookups?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A covering index contains all the columns a specific query needs — the WHERE clause key columns plus all columns in the SELECT list and ORDER BY. When a query can be satisfied entirely from the index, the optimizer performs an index-only scan without going back to the base table (no Key Lookup). You create one by adding an INCLUDE clause: CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (status) INCLUDE (amount, date) — status is the key, amount and date are stored at the leaf level for covering.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Operating in production requires knowing how the runtime or framework handles state, memory allocations, and execution locks under the hood. Failure to account for these mechanics often leads to subtle bugs that only surface under heavy load.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** A common production gotcha is unhandled edge cases during network partitions or resource exhaustion (e.g. socket exhaustion, memory grant timeouts, or unhandled promise/task rejections).

qa.q: What is a filtered index and when would you use one?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause that limits which rows are included. Example: CREATE INDEX ix_orders_pending ON orders (customer_id) WHERE status = 'pending'. This creates a small, highly selective index covering only pending orders. Benefits: smaller size, faster reads for the filtered subset, less write overhead than a full index. Use when a large table has a frequently-queried subset (active records, non-null values, specific status).

qa.q: What is the difference between REBUILD and REORGANIZE for index maintenance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** REBUILD drops and recreates the index — removes both internal and external fragmentation, updates statistics, but is an offline operation by default (blocks reads/writes) unless WITH ONLINE = ON (Enterprise edition). REORGANIZE physically reorders the leaf pages in-place — removes external fragmentation, cannot remove internal fragmentation, always online, slower for high-fragmentation cases. Rule of thumb: REORGANIZE for fragmentation 10-30%, REBUILD for > 30%.

qa.q: How do you find missing indexes in SQL Server?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Query sys.dm_db_missing_index_details joined with sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats. These DMVs track every time the query optimizer wanted an index that didn't exist, including the equality columns, inequality columns, and include columns it would have wanted. The avg_user_impact column shows the estimated % improvement. Warning: treat these as suggestions, not commands — creating every suggested index harms write performance.

qa.q: Why do too many indexes hurt performance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Every INSERT must add a row to every non-clustered index on that table. Every UPDATE to indexed columns must update those indexes. Every DELETE must remove the row from every index. A table with 10 non-clustered indexes effectively writes to 11 places (base + 10 indexes) for every INSERT. This is why OLTP tables should have fewer, carefully chosen indexes, and OLAP/reporting tables (fewer writes) can have more.
